.DISCUSSION...
Key message 1: Patchy to dense fog will impact the Monday morning 
commute. Temperatures trend warmer today and then cooler for Tuesday 
behind a cold front.

A progressive pattern continues across the CONUS with a northern 
stream trough pushing across the Great Lakes and into New England 
while a southern stream shortwave trough diving across the Desert 
Southwest. At the surface, high pressure that initially fostered the 
development of a Cold Air Damming (CAD) wedge has long since shifted 
offshore leaving behind a remnant in-situ wedge that continues to 
hang on across much of the area as a coastal low lifts into New 
England and a surface cold front approaches from the west. Copious 
boundary layer moisture from persistent drizzle will help keep areas 
of patchy fog through the mid-morning hours. An SPS for patchy to 
locally dense fog was issued for the NC mountain valleys and the SC 
Upstate earlier this morning. Locally dense fog will develop at 
times, especially in the NC Foothills and portions of the NC 
Piedmont where a Dense Fog Advisory was issued earlier this morning. 
Fog should lift around 9 AM. 

The in-situ wedge should begin to erode through the day as winds 
shift to out of the west/southwest ahead of the upstream cold front 
as it nears the mountains. Compressional warming and a return of at 
least some sunshine will support warm afternoon highs in the mid 60s 
to low 70s. The upper trough axis and surface cold front will cross 
the area late afternoon through early Tuesday morning with a 
sprawling surface high settling over the Midwest. This will usher in 
notably cooler temperatures on Tuesday with highs more seasonable 
for late November. The surface high will also shift east through the 
day across the Great Lakes and into the Mid-Atlantic which will once 
again drive the development of another CAD wedge by Tuesday night.


Key message 2: A significant storm system could impact the area 
Wednesday into Thursday bringing the potential for locally heavy 
rain and gusty winds.

The evolution of the synoptic pattern becomes much more intriguing 
Tuesday as a tall western ridge extending across the Great Basin 
amplifies downstream of a deep trough off the west coast. At the 
same time, two pieces of upper energy will be diving across the 
Rockies and ejecting into the Great Plains. A southern shortwave 
trough is progged to deepen over the Southern Plains while a 
northern trough also strengthens over the Northern Plains. A complex 
interaction between these two troughs will occur Wednesday through 
Thursday as they swing east across the Mississippi Valley and 
towards the Appalachians. Height falls from the southern wave 
overspreading a coastal baroclinic zone will help foster surface 
cyclogenesis in the vicinity of the Atlantic coast of Florida with a 
rapidly strengthening cyclone lifting across the region Wednesday 
through Thursday as the upper trough becomes negatively tilted and 
wind fields markedly intensify.

While practically all guidance depicts a notable and potentially 
significant storm system, the exact evolution of the pattern and 
resulting outcome and impacts to the region are far from certain. 
Ensemble sensitivity analysis reveals just how complex the forecast 
evolution will be, especially in regards to the interaction between 
the two upper troughs. The strength, tilt, amplitude and timing of 
both waves will have considerable impact on the forecast. The 
rainfall forecast is especially sensitive to the strength and 
amplitude of downstream ridging/blocking extending from offshore 
into portions of the Mid-Atlantic and New England. Subsequent 
ensemble clustering analysis reveals three main scenarios. The first 
scenario, which would support the greatest potential for impacts 
over the western Carolinas and northeast Georgia, depicts the 
northern upper wave evolving into a cutoff upper low over the Ohio 
Valley with a strong downstream blocking ridge. This in turn slows 
down the progression of the surface cyclone with the Ohio Valley 
cutoff low helping to draw the coastal low farther inland. In the 
second scenario, the downstream ridge isn't as strong resulting in a 
less blocked pattern allowing a more progressive solution but still 
supporting potential for the coastal low to be drawn inland. And 
finally, the third scenario has a much weaker blocking ridge and a 
weaker upper low over the Ohio Valley. This would keep the surface 
cyclone farther east along the coast with a faster progression, 
which would keep any impacts this far west more limited. As of this 
writing, the first scenario is supported by the most ensemble 
members, which are mainly comprised of the EPS and AIFS. The third 
scenario has the least support, which is mainly contributed to by 
the GEFS. 

Given the trends towards the potential for a more impactful scenario 
it's worth considering possible impacts, especially given busy 
holiday travel. A fairly strong classic CAD wedge will be in place 
Wednesday morning with a 1040mb surface high parked over New 
England. Robust deep moisture return and isentropic ascent atop the 
CAD quickly ramps up as the surface low deepens and strengthens an 
intense 60-80kt easterly low-level jet on the northern flank of the 
low. At the same time, a band of strong frontogenesis is also likely 
to develop on the northwest side of the system. Depending on the 
track of the low, this could place at least part of the area under a 
band of locally heavy rainfall with several inches of rain not out 
of the question. Given dry antecedent conditions most of this rain 
would be beneficial with minimal impact, but a focused 
frontogenetically enhanced band of rain could create localized hydro 
issues. The other impact to keep an eye on is the potential for 
gusty winds. A very tight surface pressure gradient will exist 
between the surface low (possibly sub-1000mb) and the parent high 
over New England. While exact wind gusts will depend on the strength 
and track of the surface low, gusts of 30-40mph are plausible with 
isolated power outages. In a reasonable worst case scenario gusts 
upwards of 50mph cannot be discounted with greater potential for 
power outages. The event still remains several days away so the 
reader is strongly encouraged to check back for updates as the 
forecast evolves, but indications are for a potentially messy and 
impactful Thanksgiving holiday.

A much drier and quieter pattern returns Friday through the weekend.

.AVIATION /12Z MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
At KCLT and elsewhere: Seeing a mix of MVFR to VLIFR restrictions 
across the western Carolinas terminals as of 1130Z. Restrictions 
should linger through roughly 14-16Z so have TEMPOs across the 
terminals to account for low stratus and fog. VFR expected the rest 
of the 12Z TAF period, outside of KAVL which may only see a brief 
window of VFR develop late this afternoon into early this evening. 
Winds are mostly calm to light and VRB east of the mountains this 
morning. Winds at KAVL are NW and will remain at this direction 
through the end of the TAF period. Winds will gradually increase in 
speed this evening into tonight while favoring a northerly component 
east of the mountains. Could not rule out some low-end gusts 
developing overnight into daybreak Friday east of the mountains. 
KAVL should see low-end gusts develop this afternoon, lingering 
through the end of the TAF period. 

Outlook: Dry and VFR Tuesday with breezy winds developing ahead of a 
low pressure system. The low pressure system tracks across the 
terminals Wednesday into Thursday bringing widespread rain, 
associated restrictions, and gusty winds. Drier and VFR conditions 
return Thursday night into Friday but gusty winds will continue.
